
'''Yamatohime-no-Mikoto Seiki''' (倭姫命世記) is a text believed to have been compiled in the mid-{{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|qid=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period}}.

Within ''Yamatohime-no-Mikoto Seiki,'' it is stated that the work was composed in the second year of {{ill|Jingo-keiun|en|Jingo-keiun|qid=Q1373049|lt=Jingokeiun}} (768) by "Nenge Mayumaro." However, it is widely believed to have been compiled during the mid-{{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|qid=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period}}.<ref name="#1">{{Cite web|title=倭姫命世記|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/倭姫命世記-649457|publisher=コトバンク}}</ref> It is one of the five foundational texts of {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|lt=Ise Grand Shrine|lt=Ise Shinto|ja|伊勢神道|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ise Shinto|qq=}}, the {{ill|Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shinto Gobusho|ja|神道五部書|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto Gobusho|qq=}}. The work records the traditions of {{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto|en|Yamatohime-no-mikoto|qid=Q4388732|lt=Yamatohime-no-mikoto}}, identified in the ''{{ill|Kojiki|en|Kojiki|qid=Q813031|lt=Kojiki}}'' and ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|en|Nihon Shoki|qid=Q813935|lt=Nihon Shoki}}'' as the daughter of {{ill|Emperor Suinin|en|Emperor Suinin|qid=Q314850|lt=Emperor Suinin}}, journeying across various regions with the deity {{ill|Amaterasu|en|Amaterasu|qid=Q455602|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami}} before finally enshrining her at {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|en|Ise Shrine|qid=Q687168|lt=Ise Shrine}}.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://websv.aichi-pref-library.jp/wahon/detail/54.html|title=倭姫命世記|publisher=愛知県立図書館デジタルライブラリー}}</ref><ref name="#1"/> The text also strongly asserts the doctrines of {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|lt=Ise Grand Shrine|lt=Ise Shinto|ja|伊勢神道|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ise Shinto|qq=}}.<ref name="Osumi1977p367">[[Kazuo Ōsumi]], ''Chūsei Shintō-ron'' (中世神道論), Iwanami Shoten, 1977, p. 367.</ref>

== Composition ==

The legends of ''Yamatohime-no-Mikoto Seiki'' are closely related to the expansion of {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|en|Ise Shrine|qid=Q687168|lt=Ise Shrine}}’s {{ill|Manorialism|en|Manorialism|qid=Q1550557|lt=manors}} (shōen) called ''Mikuriya'' throughout various regions from the late {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian period}} and the spread of Ise faith by lower-Ranking priests called ''Oshi'' after the {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|qid=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period}}.<ref name="#2">{{Cite web|url=https://www.bunka.pref.mie.lg.jp/saiku/hyakuwa/journal.asp?record=23|title=罪作りだよ？『倭姫命世紀』|publisher=斎宮歴史博物館}}</ref> Scholars such as {{ill|Osamu Kubota|ja|久保田収|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kubota Osamu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11369065}} have attributed its compilation to {{ill|Watarai Yukitada|ja|度会行忠|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Watarai Yukitada|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q17217919}}, though {{ill|Jun'ichi Kamata|ja|鎌田純一|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamada Junichi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11651081}} suggested that it had already been composed before Yukitada’s time.<ref name="Ban1993p5-6">Ban Gojirō, ''Kaidai,'' ''Shintō Taikei: Ise Shintō (Vol. 1)'', Shintō Taikei Hensankai, 1993, pp. 5–6.</ref> Among the medieval "Shinto Gobusho," ''Yamatohime-no-Mikoto Seiki'' is thought to have been composed relatively early, following ''{{ill|Hōki Honki|ja|宝基本紀|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hōki Honki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}},'' and further developing the philosophical ideas of that text.<ref name="Itō2012p99">[[:en:Satoshi Itō|Satoshi Itō]], ''Shintō to wa nani ka'' (神道とは何か), Chūō Kōron Shinsha, 2012, p. 99.</ref><ref name="Osumi1977p368">Kazuo Ōsumi, ''Chūsei Shintō-ron'', Iwanami Shoten, 1977, p. 368.</ref> While the attribution to Nenge Mayumaro in Jingokeiun 2 is fictional, studies by {{ill|Mikannagi Kiyonao|ja|御巫清直|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mikannagi Kiyonao|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q6537624}} have revealed that the text was based on ''{{ill|Daijingū Honki|ja|太神宮本紀|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Daijingū Honki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}},'' an ancient document of {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|en|Ise Shrine|qid=Q687168|lt=Ise Shrine}}, and incorporated traditional legends of the shrine.<ref name="Osumi1977p368"/>

Its literary style combines elements of the {{ill|Senmyō|ja|宣命体|Senmyō=Senmyō|lt=Senmyō-gata|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Senmyō|ja_comment=fixed jawiki redirect|3=宣命}} style but is not entirely consistent. The latter sections are predominantly written in a pure {{ill|Classical Chinese|en|Classical Chinese|qid=Q37041|lt=kanbun}} style with few annotations, blending classical and Kamakura-period language.<ref name="Nakamura2012p441">Nakamura Yukihiro, ''Yamatohime-no-Mikoto Seiki Kenkyū: Fukkun to Dokkai,'' Shintensha, 2012, p. 441.</ref><ref name="Nakamura2012p2-3">Nakamura Yukihiro, ''Yamatohime-no-Mikoto Seiki Kenkyū,'' pp. 2–3.</ref> The use of classical Senmyō style is considered an archaic embellishment to give the impression of antiquity.<ref name="Nakamura2012p2-3"/>

Legends of {{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto|en|Yamatohime-no-mikoto|qid=Q4388732|lt=Yamatohime-no-mikoto}} are widely recognized, and places said to have been her temporary palaces are scattered across {{ill|Gifu Prefecture|en|Gifu Prefecture|qid=Q131277|lt=Gifu Prefecture}}, {{ill|Shiga Prefecture|en|Shiga Prefecture|qid=Q131358|lt=Shiga Prefecture}}, and {{ill|Mie Prefecture|en|Mie Prefecture|qid=Q128196|lt=Mie Prefecture}}.<ref name="#2"/>

== Doctrine ==

''Yamatohime-no-Mikoto Seiki'' emphasizes {{ill|Shinto|en|Shinto|qid=Q812767|lt=Shinto}} philosophy alongside the narrative of the enshrinement of {{ill|Kōtai Jingū|ja|皇大神宮|2=ja|3=皇大神宮|4=zh|5=皇大神宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōtai Jingu|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōtai Jingū|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} by {{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto|en|Yamatohime-no-mikoto|qid=Q4388732|lt=Yamatohime-no-mikoto}}.<ref name="Osumi1977p367"/> The text records that shortly before her passing in the 23rd year of {{ill|Emperor Yūryaku|en|Emperor Yūryaku|qid=Q357235|lt=Emperor Yūryaku}}, Yamatohime-no-Mikoto delivered a divine oracle. It describes the human heart as a divine spirit, or "Shinjin," emphasizing that humans must live in a state of "Seichoku" (正直, honesty) and "Seijō" (清浄, purity).<ref name="KaifuMitsuhashi2018p105-107">Kaifu Yawotome & Mitsuhashi Ken, ''Yamatohime-no-Mikoto-sama no Monogatari,'' Fuyōsha International, 2018, pp. 105–107.</ref> 

Another oracle, "Return to the origin, and align yourself with the fundamental essence," conveys the idea of renewal through recognizing and restoring one’s connection to the source, a concept known as ''Motomoto Honhon.'' This philosophy resonates with the rituals of the {{ill|Jingū Shikinen Sengū|lt=Jingū Shikinen Sengū|lt=Shikinen Sengu|ja|式年遷宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shikinen Sengu|ja_comment=fixed jawiki redirect|3=遷宮}}.<ref name="SakamotoIshii2011p55">Sakamoto Koremaru & Ishii Kenji, ''Prestep Shintōgaku,'' Kōbundō, 2011, p. 55.</ref>

== Research History ==

Empirical research on the ''Shinto Gobusho'' began with the Edo-period scholar {{ill|Yoshimi Yoshikazu|ja|吉見幸和|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshimi Yukikazu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q63131320}} in ''Gobusho Setsuben'' (1736). Yukikazu criticized ''Yamatohime-no-Mikoto Seiki'' as the latest among the ''Gobusho,'' claiming it was a medieval fabrication by {{ill|Kōtai Jingū|lt=Kōtai Jingū|lt=Outer Shrine|ja|外宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Outer Shrine|ja_comment=fixed jawiki redirect|3=豊受大神宮}} priests.<ref name="Osumi1977p368"/> However, later scholars such as {{ill|Motoori Norinaga|en|Motoori Norinaga|qid=Q384647|lt=Motoori Norinaga}} recognized the inclusion of ancient {{ill|Ise traditions|ja|伊勢伝承|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ise traditions|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in the text. Further analysis by {{ill|Mikannagi Kiyonao|ja|御巫清直|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mikannagi Kiyonao|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q6537624}} demonstrated its basis in ''{{ill|Daijingū Honki|ja|太神宮本紀|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Daijingū Honki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.'' Postwar research by scholars like {{ill|Okada Yoneo|ja|岡田米男|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Okada Yoneo|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, {{ill|Nishida Osamu|ja|西田長男|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nishida Osamu|qq=}}, and {{ill|Osamu Kubota|ja|久保田収|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kubota Osamu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11369065}} further refined understanding of the text’s origins and its incorporation of ancient traditions.<ref name="Osumi1977p368"/>
